utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm afraid that I have to say that I do hear you. Unfortunately I don't understand anything today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean? Why is that? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] The case happened -- the same case happened once again when I learned that another investigator received a letter with the question why he was working in Banja Luka. I think that this is something you can exert your influence to. I don't know why attempts are being made to influence in an adverse manner my defence. I have had this Defence for quite a while, and I do not want my Defence team to be attacked in any way. I am very concerned. I have been reading regularly all of the papers that you have sent me via the Office of the Prosecutor. I couldn't follow anything yesterday because I couldn't concentrate myself. There are serious things happening, and I am indeed very concerned. This goes to the issue of my lawyer, and I really had to draw your attention to this problem. Thank you very much for having listened to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... with your lawyer? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] This incident that I learned about today, that the second investigator also received a similar letter, is something that I learned about only an hour ago, and -- over the telephone. Anyway, this is something that I know we discussed yesterday. But this new incident has only exacerbated the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which -- you're referring to a second investigator? It may be a problem of translation. Perhaps Mr. Ackerman can help me there. We're talking of investigators. What are we talking about? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] I am talking about the legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I have a clarification on what your client is actually referring to. He's just saying that he's received some information today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can only tell you what I think it is, Your Honour. I have haven't communicated with him today, so I don't know where he received information. But what -- what I saw today was a letter from the Registrar saying that they were denying one of my investigator's trips from his home to Banja Luka to work during the first -- 1st through the 16th of this month because there was no justification for his being in Banja Luka. And I wrote a response to that that we're in the Banja Luka phase of the case and it's Banja Luka matters that are going on and I need to have Banja Luka matters investigated during this period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is all news to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was news to me until five minutes ago, Your Honour. So -- but it's -- it's the kind of thing we do deal with on occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, you've heard me say this is all news to me. And in simple language, that means that this is the first time I'm hearing about it, which brings me to tell you that I have no comments to make at this present moment until I get more information about the matter. What I can put -- what I can assure you of is that if there is any irregularity, I will put it right. If what is being done is according to the rules and regulations of this Tribunal, then it will have to be that way. But if it's not according to the rules and regulations of this Tribunal, or if it ridicules or renders into nothing your rights as a defendant in this case, then I will do something about it. But until I get more information, there's very little I can tell you and in fact I'm not going to tell you any more. THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Is there anything else you would like to tell me -- or tell us, I mean? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] No. Your Honour, I'm really sorry that I had to say what I said. Usually I don't speak on my own. I do it through my lawyer. But I really felt the need to address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, I appreciate two things that you have just said. First, that what you have to say you usually say it through your lawyer. And I can assure you that you have got a very capable lawyer defending you who is definitely not going to stop short of telling the Court what he thinks that he needs to tell the Court. That's number one. And secondly, I also want to assure you or -- and also encourage you that if there is anything in the course of the trial that you don't like, that you have reservations about, which you think that can influence your right to a fair trial, please do come forward. Don't hesitate for a moment. No one is going to shout at you or shut your mouth and tell you to keep quiet, because you have every right to a fair trial before this Tribunal, and you will get a fair trial. So that if there is anything that you have reservations about, even if there are things that you may be in disagreement with your Defence counsel, you have every right to stand up and inform the Tribunal about it. And you will be heard. THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. General Talic -- I'm not hinting, Mr. Ackerman, that there may be some kind of disagreement. But you are a senior lawyer, and you know that that sort of thing happens every now and then, and sometimes it's thanks to the Court itself that things are sorted out and smoothed out. General Talic, good afternoon to you. THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you hear me -- THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any kind of problems that your colleague, Mr. Brdjanin, has or can I ask you to sit down and get over and done with? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] I have nothing to raise, Your Honour. I have no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and we can -- I suppose, Mr. Cayley, if you have nothing to put, we can call the witness in. Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one matter. And maybe it's -- I'm the only person in the room that misunderstood. Yesterday when we were talking about the witness who had been interviewed by my co-counsel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Chamber -- you, Your Honour, asked Ms. Korner if it was a protected witness. I had the impression that she had told you that it was a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She did tell me that he had asked initially to be afforded all the protective measures, including pseudonym and I don't remember what else. But Ms. Korner was very clear about it. He was a protected witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I went home and looked for motions and orders in that regard, and -- and then I took it up with the Prosecutor today and there aren't any. They hadn't made any request for protection nor any orders for protection regarding this witness at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, are you familiar with the details of what Mr. Ackerman has just stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Mr. Ackerman raised this with me before you came into court and my understanding is hat we have not made full application for specific measures in respect of any of the witnesses from that particular municipality as yet. So if that was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I also heard Ms. Korner state in no unclear terms yesterday that the particular witness had asked for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is correct. But we -- when we make an application for protective measures, we do it per municipality. So when we're coming up to a municipality, we put in an application in respect of all those witnesses in that municipality. If she stated that, she may well have been referring to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She definitely did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly. Your recollection is better than mine, Your Honour. If she stated that, she may well have been referring to either, one, the general order that is in place in respect of all witnesses; and two, the fact that this individual had asked the Office of the Prosecutor if protective measures could be put in place prior to his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I got the impression from Ms. Korner that following the occurrence of this recent development that we discussed yesterday in closed session, he definitely reiterated his request for protective measures but that he had requested protective measures in the first place sometime back when he was first asked to cooperate with this Tribunal. I suppose that more or less the importance of this issue will arise or will have a place when we hand down the -- our decision following what was discussed yesterday. And it will obviously have a bearing on the decision that will be taken later on as -- in a second stage, following any investigations that we might order. However, it is of concern to us as a Trial Chamber to know that simply because a municipality had not yet appeared on the scene, on the horizon, a question of protective measures is put in abeyance. Because you can -- you're intelligent enough to read through what I'm saying very quickly and see what the consequences could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I mean, Your Honour, I hear what you're saying. With respect, the measures apply generally to protection within the Tribunal and within the actual courtroom in respect of facial distortion or voice distortion or closed session. That's why it is carried out in that matter. We can certainly discuss it amongst ourselves after the hearing today and maybe think about putting them en bloc for all of the upcoming witnesses. The only problem with that of course is that some witnesses fall away. We never have a final list of witnesses, as happened in Banja Luka. Not every witness attends in the end for various reasons, so it can change before we actually get to the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I mean to say is that you can have, from what I can se see, a situation obtaining whereby you have during the pre-trial stage a declaration or a list of the witnesses that the Prosecution intends to bring forward in a case, and that list includes persons who have either sought already or who might be seeking protective measures with the obvious consequences, unforeseen unfortunately most of the time, that we are encountering in this case without my need to go into any specific details. And it changes the picture, the whole scenario.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because if one -- if the name of a particular witness was listed in the course of the pre-trial stage when the Prosecution was bound by the rules to provide the details of the evidence to -- it intended to bring forward, and that list included the name of a person who had already either sought protection or intended to seek -- or was likely to seek protective measures, it could potentially create big, big problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That particular document, I believe, is under seal, the Rule 65 summaries, because of that problem. But I can check that. In other words, the summaries of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I would tend to agree with you that it is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. So that is not released to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it doesn't make sense either, then, if you intend to bring forward witnesses 1 to 10, and you provide the name under seal and then you file later on motions not to have the name of those particular witnesses disclosed to the Defence prior to 21 days before that witness being summoned in, et cetera, et cetera. So I think this is something that ought to be examined by the OTP and looked into deeply, I would suppose, because it could create problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But recall, Your Honour, that there is a general order in place. Mr. Ackerman is complying with and we in fact spoke to each other about it, that the Defence are obliged not to disclose to third parties any of these statements. That applies to all of the witness statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is overboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: All of the witness statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is overboard, no question about, it there is no question about it, but what I mean to say is that there are instances that you know about as a Prosecutor in this case and in previous cases whereby in order to have an effective protective measure in favour of a particular witness, you ask your -- or request the Chamber to effectively make sure that the Defence is denied information on a particular witness before or until a particular date. Whether that is in compliance or conformity or lives along with the system that we have adopting -- we have been adopting so far, I don't know. I mean, it's a question that I'm inviting you as -- as a senior member of the OTP to go into and make sure that the two go together like a horse and carriage, because otherwise we are -- we are in troubled waters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, Your Honour. Relating to the issue that we discussed yesterday, it does create --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The problem is not Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman now with his clean bill of health is even less of a problem than he was before. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem I think you have hit the nail on the head, so to speak, is this: That we have an obligation to conduct investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And there are witnesses who come here to testify who don't care if the whole world knows that they are testifying. We've had some of those. There are others who care a great deal and it makes a difference as to how we approach an investigation with regard to a particular witness, how that witness feels about those kinds of issues. We have no way of knowing what those witnesses have told the Prosecutor about their circumstances, whether or not they are in a position where they believe they might be in danger, all those kinds of things. We don't know those things. We have no reason to believe -- or had no reason to believe, after I looked last night and discovered that there was no protective measures regarding this particular witness we talked about yesterday that had been requested. And apparently this is a -- well, I better not talk about it because we're in open session. But we cannot be held to a particular standard with regard to particular witnesses if we're deprived of the information that is crucial to the way we conduct an investigation. That's the point that I think you have seized upon and the point that's important to have resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, let's -- Mr. Ackerman, let's put the dots on the I's in no uncertain terms. I don't think in all fairness that the Prosecution at any given time in any given moment yesterday denied you the right to interview witnesses of the Prosecution. When I say "of the Prosecution," it's relatively speaking, because Ms. Korner herself conceded that there's no ownership with regard to witnesses. So that's not -- that's not the issue. The issue is the line of demarcation, the moment you decide to approach a witness that you know is one of the witnesses that the Prosecution is bringing forward is -- you have to be diligent, clever, wise enough to know where the line of demarcation is. If you trespass that line, don't expect this Trial Chamber to be lenient or to be nice with you. We will come down on you, your Defence team, or on the Defence team of General Talic with all the weight that we can carry, definitely, if you trespass the line. But you definitely have the right, and you are expected as a good Defence counsel to do your job well. And this Trial Chamber will not interfere with your work, provided you do not trespass the line. I will obviously not tell you where the line of demarcation is, because this may be something that we need to discuss or to decide upon later on. But there is definitely a line of demarcation, because approaching the witnesses of the Prosecution is one thing; bearing undue influence on those witnesses or doing anything that is forbidden by the Rules with regard to -- vis a vis those witnesses is another, and I don't need to amplify on that. But I don't think that is what we are talking about. You realise, and you are a senior lawyer here as well, to know Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. well enough there may be -- that there may be instances where the Prosecution is perfectly entitled to appeal to this Trial Chamber for special protective measures protecting particular witnesses or may be exposed to particular danger given certain circumstances. And I have the impression -- I got this impression from one of the very early hearings -- sittings in this Trial Chamber -- that you are very cooperative in this, Mr. Ackerman, and I have no reason to doubt your cooperation. In those circumstances, it is the duty of this Trial Chamber to take all the necessary precautions not to expose these possible potential witnesses to unnecessary personal risk or personal danger, anyway. And the Prosecution will find the cooperation of this Tribunal in that. And I would understand -- I would anticipate the Defence to be cooperative. And I'm sure that I can expect that from you. What you can also rest assured of is that there is no way -- and I have made this clear to the Prosecution already -- that there is no way that you can be asked to prepare adequately for your client's defence without being provided with all the opportunities necessary. So if basically we come to a stage where we have to keep protected the name of a particular witness or the details of a particular witness, et cetera, the disclosure will take place in good time to enable you to prepare for an adequate defence, and the Tribunal also will consider any submissions that you may have to make sure that you will have every opportunity to prepare for an adequate defence. But you also need to cooperate with the Tribunal in securing all the precautionary measures that need to be put in place if and when they are necessary with regard to particular witnesses. That I'm making clear to the Prosecution, as well as to you. And I don't -- I mean, you're free to say what you saw, what you like, and to make the submissions that you like, but this is a position which the Tribunal feels very strong about. I mean, the Tribunal feels very strongly about -- not about you or any one of your colleagues approaching any of the witnesses of the Prosecution. That's neither here nor there. It's the way it's done. It's what it's -- what is said. It isn't necessarily what the witness thinks. It's what happens on that particular occasion if the information is forthcoming, because sometime it may not even be forthcoming. But it's -- you're invited to -- if what Ms. Korner said yesterday is correct, that is, that in the initial stages or at some point in time you said that as a lead counsel you were in control of what was happening in -- in Banja Luka or in the territory of ex-Yugoslavia, then what is expected from you is a very simple thing: Stay in control, make sure that the line of demarcation, the frontier is not trespassed. If a mistake is done there, there's a price to pay. And I think I'm being clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate very much -- and I think we all do -- the clarification. In your last comment, President Truman used to have on his desk a little plaque that said, "The buck stops here." And has lead counsel, that's my position, I am responsible for what the people who work for me do. I try to give them the best instructions I can and hope that they're followed. That's the best I can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Anything else from you, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No. Mr. President, you've said everything on this issue. I don't need to add anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we can bring the witness in. Usher, please. Yes, we'll go into closed session, please, before. Make sure that the gentleman does not come into the courtroom, this beautiful courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: reconvened on Wednesday, the 10th day of April, 2002, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00, to be
